language.note: Iran's census does not ask language. The language figures this map shows for Iran are population-weighted sums of the settlement estimates in the Atlas of the Languages of Iran, a research atlas published province by province. gap_reason: Language: no Iranian census has ever asked it. Some provinces and counties carry a figure all the same -- a population-weighted roll-up of the settlement estimates in the Atlas of the Languages of Iran, marked as the atlas's field estimates and not as anybody's count. The atlas is published province by province and has reached twelve of the thirty-one; the rest of the country is empty because those modules do not exist yet, and Kermanshah is empty because its module reaches five of its fourteen counties and under a fifth of its people. Religion is a different gap: the 2016 census asked it and the Statistical Centre publishes it by province only, so no county carries it.
median_age_note: Interpolated within the single year of age that holds the middle person, from Table 1 of the 2016 census (population by single year of age and sex).
ethnicity_note: Country of citizenship, from Table 3 of the 2016 census (population by sex and citizenship): Iranian nationals and the nationals of each other country the Centre tabulates. Iran's census does not ask ethnicity, so the citizenship it counts is shown in its place, as Japan's and Korea's nationality is. It is citizenship, not ethnic group: every Iranian citizen, whatever their ethnicity, is an 'Iranian national' here.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Abdanan County itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 61 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 46,591 people, 99.2% of the atlas's own total for Abdanan County, 46,977 people in the 2011 census. 16 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Gheitasi, Mojtaba, Erik Anonby, et al. (2017), and the rows themselves cite Mojtaba Gheitasi, field notes 2016.

sources.name: Gheitasi, Mojtaba, Erik Anonby, et al. (2017). Language distribution in Ilam Province, Iran. In Erik Anonby, Mortaza Taheri-Ardali, et al. (eds.), Atlas of the Languages of Iran (ALI). Ottawa: GCRC (Geomatics and Cartographic Research Centre), Carleton University.

language.method: population-weighted sum of every published ALI settlement estimate in the unit
language.note: Nothing was read for Amlash itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 125 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2016 census population where the atlas prints one and the 2011 census population otherwise. Those weighted places hold 43,150 people, 99.8% of the atlas's own total for Amlash, 43,225 people in the 2016 census. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Poshtvan, Hamideh, Erik Anonby, et al. (2022), and the rows themselves cite Hamideh Poshtvan, field notes 2021.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Badreh itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 28 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 16,048 people, 99.7% of the atlas's own total for Badreh, 16,096 people in the 2011 census. 4 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Gheitasi, Mojtaba, Erik Anonby, et al. (2017), and the rows themselves cite Mojtaba Gheitasi, field notes 2016.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Dalahu itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 158 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 39,215 people, 98.4% of the atlas's own total for Dalahu, 39,837 people in the 2011 census. 13 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Fattahi, Mehdi, Erik Anonby, et al. (2022), and the rows themselves cite Mehdi Fattahi, field notes 2017. The module is dated 2022, but the fieldwork behind it is older: the rows cite field notes of 2017, and 100% of the people weighted here sit behind notes taken 3 or more years before the module was published.

sources.name: Fattahi, Mehdi, Erik Anonby, et al. (2022). Language distribution in Kermanshah Province, Iran. In Erik Anonby, Mortaza Taheri-Ardali, et al. (eds.), Atlas of the Languages of Iran (ALI). Ottawa: GCRC (Geomatics and Cartographic Research Centre), Carleton University.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Genaveh itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 55 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 90,432 people, 99.9% of the atlas's own total for Genaveh, 90,493 people in the 2011 census. 9 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Nemati, Fatemeh, Shakiba Ghasemi, Erik Anonby, et al. (2017), and the rows themselves cite Fatemeh Nemati and Shakiba Ghasemi, field notes 2017; Maryam Nourzaei, field notes 2014. The module is dated 2017, but the fieldwork behind it is older: the rows cite field notes of 2014-2017, and 44% of the people weighted here sit behind notes taken 3 or more years before the module was published.

No table of religion by shahrestan is among the Centre's archived detailed census tables (population tables 1, 2, 3 and 9; activity, households, housing, migration, education, marriage), so no share is written below the province.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Jam itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 84 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 51,373 people, 99.9% of the atlas's own total for Jam, 51,446 people in the 2011 census. 11 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Nemati, Fatemeh, Shakiba Ghasemi, Erik Anonby, et al. (2017), and the rows themselves cite Fatemeh Nemati and Shakiba Ghasemi, field notes 2017; Maryam Nourzaei, field notes 2014. The module is dated 2017, but the fieldwork behind it is older: the rows cite field notes of 2014-2017, and 24% of the people weighted here sit behind notes taken 3 or more years before the module was published.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Kabutarahang itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 129 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 131,526 people, 104.3% of the 126,062 people this map gives the unit. The weighted settlements hold 5,464 people more than that total, 4.3% of it: the atlas's settlement populations and the population this map gives the unit do not quite agree, and neither has been adjusted to the other. 1 further settlement carries a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Izadi, Elham, Mehrdad Meshkinfam, Erik Anonby, et al. (2021), and the rows themselves cite Mehrdad Meshkinfam and Elham Izadi, field notes 2020.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Khamir itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 66 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 52,522 people, 99.2% of the atlas's own total for Khamir, 52,968 people in the 2011 census. 7 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Mohebbi Bahmani, Hassan, Ali Rashidi, Erik Anonby, et al. (2015), and the rows themselves cite Ali Rashidi, pers. comm. 2015; Maryam Nourzaei, field notes 2011. The module is dated 2015, but the fieldwork behind it is older: the rows cite field notes of 2011-2015, and 22% of the people weighted here sit behind notes taken 3 or more years before the module was published.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Khomeini Shahr itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 8 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 311,627 people, 100.0% of the atlas's own total for Khomeini Shahr, 311,629 people in the 2011 census. 1 further settlement carries a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Talebi-Dastenaei, Mahnaz, Habib Borjian, Erik Anonby, et al. (2022), and the rows themselves cite Saber Bakhtiari and Mahnaz Talebi-Dastenaei, field notes 2020.

sources.name: Talebi-Dastenaei, Mahnaz, Habib Borjian, Erik Anonby, et al. (2022). Language distribution in Esfahan Province, Iran. In Erik Anonby, Mortaza Taheri-Ardali, et al. (eds.), Atlas of the Languages of Iran (ALI). Ottawa: GCRC (Geomatics and Cartographic Research Centre), Carleton University.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Lenjan itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 56 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 246,495 people, 100.0% of the atlas's own total for Lenjan, 246,510 people in the 2011 census. 3 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Talebi-Dastenaei, Mahnaz, Habib Borjian, Erik Anonby, et al. (2022), and the rows themselves cite Reyhaneh Salimian and Mortaza Taheri-Ardali, field notes 2021.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Minab itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 254 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 235,636 people, 100.0% of the atlas's own total for Minab, 235,705 people in the 2011 census. 10 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. The module is Mohebbi Bahmani, Hassan, Ali Rashidi, Erik Anonby, et al. (2015), and the rows themselves cite Hassan Mohebbi Bahmani, field notes 2015; Maryam Nourzaei, field notes 2011.

gap_reason: Language: no Iranian census has ever asked it. Some provinces and counties carry a figure all the same -- a population-weighted roll-up of the settlement estimates in the Atlas of the Languages of Iran, marked as the atlas's field estimates and not as anybody's count. The atlas is published province by province and has reached twelve of the thirty-one; the rest of the country is empty because those modules do not exist yet, and Kermanshah is empty because its module reaches five of its fourteen counties and under a fifth of its people. Religion is a different gap: the 2016 census asked it and the Statistical Centre publishes it by province only, so no county carries it.
median_age_note: Interpolated within the single year of age that holds the middle person, from Table 1 of the 2016 census (population by single year of age and sex).
ethnicity_note: Country of citizenship, from Table 3 of the 2016 census (population by sex and citizenship): Iranian nationals and the nationals of each other country the Centre tabulates. Iran's census does not ask ethnicity, so the citizenship it counts is shown in its place, as Japan's and Korea's nationality is. It is citizenship, not ethnic group: every Iranian citizen, whatever their ethnicity, is an 'Iranian national' here.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Parsian itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 43 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 42,837 people, 100.0% of the atlas's own total for Parsian, 42,843 people in the 2011 census. 1 further settlement carries a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Mohebbi Bahmani, Hassan, Ali Rashidi, Erik Anonby, et al. (2015), and the rows themselves cite Ali Rashidi, pers. comm. 2015; Maryam Nourzaei, field notes 2011; Mortaza Taheri, field notes 2017. The module is dated 2015, but the fieldwork behind it is older: the rows cite field notes of 2011-2015, and 23% of the people weighted here sit behind notes taken 3 or more years before the module was published.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Qasr-e-Shirin itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 81 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 24,239 people, 95.0% of the atlas's own total for Qasr-e-Shirin, 25,517 people in the 2011 census. 43 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Fattahi, Mehdi, Erik Anonby, et al. (2022), and the rows themselves cite Mehdi Fattahi, field notes 2017. The module is dated 2022, but the fieldwork behind it is older: the rows cite field notes of 2017, and 100% of the people weighted here sit behind notes taken 3 or more years before the module was published.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Razan itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 126 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 113,329 people, 105.3% of the 107,587 people this map gives the unit. The weighted settlements hold 5,742 people more than that total, 5.3% of it: the atlas's settlement populations and the population this map gives the unit do not quite agree, and neither has been adjusted to the other. 3 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Izadi, Elham, Mehrdad Meshkinfam, Erik Anonby, et al. (2021), and the rows themselves cite Mehrdad Meshkinfam and Elham Izadi, field notes 2020.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Sarpol-e-Zahab itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 175 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 85,105 people, 99.4% of the atlas's own total for Sarpol-e-Zahab, 85,616 people in the 2011 census. 9 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Fattahi, Mehdi, Erik Anonby, et al. (2022), and the rows themselves cite Mehdi Fattahi, field notes 2017. The module is dated 2022, but the fieldwork behind it is older: the rows cite field notes of 2017, and 100% of the people weighted here sit behind notes taken 3 or more years before the module was published.

sources.name: Fattahi, Mehdi, Erik Anonby, et al. (2022). Language distribution in Kermanshah Province, Iran. In Erik Anonby, Mortaza Taheri-Ardali, et al. (eds.), Atlas of the Languages of Iran (ALI). Ottawa: GCRC (Geomatics and Cartographic Research Centre), Carleton University.

language.method: population-weighted sum of every published ALI settlement estimate in the unit
language.note: Nothing was read for Sharekurd itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 29 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 275,006 people, 100.0% of the 275,006 left of the atlas's total for Sharekurd (340,382 people in the 2011 census) once the 29,481 it counts in Ben and the 35,895 in Saman, which the map draws apart, are taken out. This map gives the polygon 315,980 people (2016); the weighted places are 87.0% of that. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Taheri-Ardali, Mortaza, Erik Anonby, et al. (2015), and the rows themselves cite Morteza Taheri, field notes 2015.

language.method: population-weighted sum of every published ALI settlement estimate in the unit
language.note: Nothing was read for Sowme'eh Sara itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 153 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2016 census population where the atlas prints one and the 2011 census population otherwise. Those weighted places hold 124,904 people, 99.9% of the atlas's own total for Sowme'eh Sara, 125,074 people in the 2016 census. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Poshtvan, Hamideh, Erik Anonby, et al. (2022), and the rows themselves cite Hamideh Poshtvan, field notes 2021.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Tuyserkan itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 107 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 103,083 people, 101.4% of the 101,666 people this map gives the unit. The weighted settlements hold 1,417 people more than that total, 1.4% of it: the atlas's settlement populations and the population this map gives the unit do not quite agree, and neither has been adjusted to the other. 2 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Izadi, Elham, Mehrdad Meshkinfam, Erik Anonby, et al. (2021), and the rows themselves cite Mehrdad Meshkinfam and Elham Izadi, field notes 2020.
